cells.text: Chapters 1–4 build the agent from first principles: agency, control loops, context, memory, tools, and interoperability.
Chapters 5–6 explain coordination, multi-agent designs, durable runtimes, tracing, budgets, and production operations.
Chapters 7–8 turn reliability, evaluation, security, privacy, and governance into engineering disciplines.
Chapters 9–11 connect use-case selection, product economics, sales, frameworks, and a production reference architecture.
Chapter 12 examines long-horizon control, learning from experience, verification, automated science, and agent institutions.
The model produces text. The application decides what, if anything, to do with it.
The model contributes to a path whose transitions are mostly chosen by code.
The model chooses among tools and steps, but permissions, budgets, and stopping rules are explicit.
The model can create longer plans, adapt strategy, and recover across a broad action space. Evaluation and control become correspondingly harder.
Who may define or modify the objective?
Can the model create or revise multi-step plans?
Which tools and side effects may the model invoke?
How long may it continue without human review?
What time, token, money, compute, or API budgets may it spend?
May it call subagents or remote agents, and under what identity?
What may it persist, update, or forget across sessions?
Choose the next action from current state. Best when useful information arrives incrementally.
Create an explicit decomposition, then execute and revise. Useful for dependency-rich tasks.
Explore multiple candidate paths and select among them. Useful when early choices dominate outcome quality.
Use failure evidence to improve a subsequent attempt. Most valuable when feedback is externally grounded.
Generate a compact program that performs many low-level operations. Powerful but requires strong sandboxing.
Use code for identity, permissions, budgets, transaction semantics, and hard business rules.
Use routing where categories are semantic and numerous, but each downstream path can remain narrow.
Name phases and persist state when tasks are long-running, interruptible, or operationally important.
Attach a narrow evaluator to a risk or quality dimension rather than asking one model to judge everything.
Spend extra inference only when independent exploration has plausible marginal value.
Only the information needed for the next decision or short local plan.
Versioned instructions that can constrain action; kept distinct from ordinary retrieved content.
Facts or documents with source, time, and ideally confidence or validation metadata.
Compressed prior interaction used for continuity, never treated as a substitute for original evidence.
Only capabilities currently permitted and relevant to the task phase.
Who or what is allowed to persist a new memory?
What outcome, source, or human confirmation is required before promotion?
Is the memory task-specific, user-specific, organization-wide, or global?
When does the memory expire, get revalidated, or get deleted?
How can a wrong memory be superseded without leaving ambiguous copies?
Which agents, users, or tools may retrieve it?
Lowest operational risk; still validate authorization, privacy, and source freshness.
Allow only with clear before/after state and reliable rollback semantics.
Require stronger policy gates, confirmation, transaction identity, and audit evidence.
Expect partial observability, timing issues, and post-action verification.
Treat the sandbox boundary as a security product, not as a convenience wrapper.
Connect an agent to tools, resources, and data-oriented capabilities. Think vertical integration.
Connect independently operated agents that can accept tasks and collaborate. Think horizontal delegation.
Authenticates users, services, and delegated actors; should not be inferred from protocol discovery.
Decides whether a capability may be used in the current context, regardless of whether it is discoverable.
Records calls, tasks, artifacts, errors, and provenance across protocol boundaries.
Use when decomposition is natural and the manager can integrate bounded results.
Use when responsibility, tools, or policy genuinely move to a specialist.
Use when a specialist produces a bounded artifact while the caller retains responsibility.
Use when multiple perspectives have genuinely different evidence or error profiles.
Use when information gathering is separable and latency matters enough to justify duplicate context cost.
Use shared task state and explicit ownership of subtasks.
Version observations and reject writes based on outdated state.
Carry identity and delegated permissions with every task, not merely in prose.
Preserve source lineage so repeated claims are not mistaken for independent evidence.
Route artifacts and summaries to the agents that need them rather than broadcasting context.
Bound privileges, limit fan-out, and add circuit breakers between autonomous actors.
Persist the state required to resume without reconstructing the task from memory.
Ensure a retry does not duplicate an external side effect.
Buffer work and control concurrency, priority, and rate-limited dependencies.
Pause at a meaningful state and resume with human or external input.
When execution outcome is uncertain, query real state before deciding what to do next.
Connect model decisions, tools, state, artifacts, guardrails, and humans in one run history.
Measure whether the real task reached the intended end state, not merely whether text looked good.
Track tokens, tool calls, latency, compute, browser steps, and human-review cost.
Classify recurring causes so production incidents become regression tests.
Reconstruct a failed run with the same or modified state to understand and test corrections.
Did the external system reach the intended and authorized state?
Were evidence gathering, tool choices, ordering, and stopping behavior reasonable?
Did the run respect authorization, privacy, business rules, and approval requirements?
Does the same case succeed across repeated runs rather than only occasionally?
Can the agent handle tool errors, ambiguous input, changed state, and interrupted execution?
What does a successful outcome cost in time, tokens, tool calls, and human attention?
Realistic web navigation and action; useful for understanding browser-agent fragility.
Long-horizon professional computer use; exposes state tracking, verification, and recovery gaps.
General assistant tasks requiring reasoning, search, and tool use.
Repository-level software engineering with human-validated issue instances.
Tool-agent-user interaction with domain policies and repeatability metrics.
The only benchmark that directly represents your policies, tools, data, and economics.
Untrusted text manipulates the agent into pursuing an attacker-selected objective.
A legitimate capability is invoked with unsafe intent, sequence, or parameters.
Credentials or delegated authority exceed the actor, task, or time scope actually required.
Tools, skills, servers, agents, or prompts are compromised or change unexpectedly.
Natural-language or tool paths lead to unsafe code or command execution.
Untrusted or incorrect information becomes durable and influences future runs.
One compromised or mistaken component propagates bad state through dependent agents.
Minimize capabilities, separate trust classes, isolate risky execution.
Apply authorization and guardrails at tool and transaction boundaries.
Minimize context, scope traces and memory, enforce retention and deletion.
Maintain adversarial tests, regression results, and release history.
Preserve traces, approvals, incidents, and remediation actions.
Map the deployed use case and organizational role to applicable obligations rather than relying on model branding.
Strong tool access, executable feedback, sandboxing, and testable end states make iterative agents effective.
Conversation, knowledge, and transactions combine; clear handoff and resolution outcomes support deployment and pricing.
Rich telemetry and APIs support diagnosis; mutation risk argues for asymmetric permissions and approvals.
Search and synthesis benefit from agents, but evaluation requires provenance, source quality, and epistemic caution.
Agents can accelerate investigation, but privilege, adversarial input, and evidence preservation demand strict controls.
Can the agent see the information needed to understand current state?
Are useful operations available through stable tools or controllable computer-use environments?
Can the organization determine whether the task actually succeeded?
Can mistakes be detected, reversed, or escalated before major harm?
Can permissions, budgets, and approval points be expressed concretely?
Is the workflow valuable enough to fund integration, inference, evaluation, and oversight?
Usually buy or support several providers unless model research is itself the business.
Use as an implementation accelerator; avoid making framework-specific abstractions the core moat.
Often strategic in enterprises because identity, policy, routing, budgets, and governance accumulate here.
Frequently strategic because they encode real workflow semantics and safe action boundaries.
Strong candidate for ownership: it represents task reality, failure history, and quality expectations.
Valuable when linked to trajectories, outcomes, and expert corrections rather than stored as undifferentiated logs.
Best for employee augmentation where value accrues continuously across many tasks.
Useful for platforms with heterogeneous model and tool usage.
Fits workflows where discrete tool-backed operations are the natural unit.
Fits service interactions, though conversation length and value can vary substantially.
Strong alignment when success is objectively measurable and attribution is clear.
Useful when buyers require budget predictability and the vendor can manage usage risk.
Compact agent abstraction with tools, handoffs, guardrails, sessions, MCP, tracing, and structured outputs.
Enterprise-oriented .NET/Python framework unifying AutoGen/Semantic Kernel directions; strong Microsoft ecosystem fit.
Multi-language, tool- and workflow-oriented stack with evaluation, sandbox execution, deployment, and A2A support.
Low-level graph runtime emphasizing durable state, checkpoints, interrupts, replay, and explicit control.
High-level role-oriented multi-agent abstractions plus structured Flows for bounded orchestration.
Appropriate when requirements are narrow, highly regulated, latency-sensitive, or when framework abstraction adds more risk than value.
Turn a user request into a durable task with identity, objective, and applicable policy.
Assemble minimal sufficient state with provenance and an explicitly limited tool surface.
Use the model to choose among allowed actions or produce bounded artifacts.
Enforce model routing, permissions, budgets, guardrails, escalation, and policy.
Persist state, manage queues and retries, pause for humans, and resume safely.
Execute typed actions with scoped identities, transaction semantics, and isolation.
Continuously test task outcomes, trajectories, safety, cost, and production drift.
Represent goals and checks at multiple timescales to reduce drift in very long tasks.
Promote reusable lessons only through validated outcome signals and controlled memory updates.
Maintain structured state that captures entities, constraints, temporal relationships, and expected effects.
Combine model interpretation with deterministic solvers, rules, types, tests, or formal checks.
Ask the agent to search for disconfirming evidence rather than only supporting its current plan.
Long-lived actors that maintain state and responsibilities across projects and teams.
Systems that connect literature, hypotheses, experiments, evidence, and critique rather than only generating papers.
Specialists discoverable through protocols, with identity, payment, reputation, and service guarantees.
Governance mechanisms designed for interactions that may occur far faster and at larger scale than human oversight.
Research processes in which claims, evidence, provenance, tests, and revision become partly machine-operable objects.
Is the business or research outcome observable independently of the model’s own explanation?
Which task classes are in scope, and which must be rejected or escalated?
Which actions can change external state, under which identity, and with which maximum privilege?
Are tool schemas narrow, typed, versioned, and explicit about side effects and errors?
Does the model see only task-relevant information that the current identity is authorized to access?
Can the task resume after failure without reconstructing critical facts from a chat transcript?
Who is allowed to write long-term memory, how is provenance stored, and how are corrections and deletion handled?
Does the evaluation suite include realistic outcomes, repeated trials, trajectories, adversarial cases, and cost?
Can untrusted content influence reasoning without acquiring authority, credentials, memory-write access, or network reach?
Are approvals placed before consequential transitions rather than indiscriminately around every model call?
Can an incident be reconstructed from identity, context, model version, tool calls, state, policy decisions, and external effects?
Is cost measured per verified outcome, including retries, tools, infrastructure, and human intervention?
Do model, prompt, retrieval, tool, policy, and memory changes trigger relevant regression evaluations?
When the agent cannot complete safely, does it fail legibly into a useful human or deterministic process?
A system in which a model can influence the sequence of actions used to pursue a goal in an environment.
The repeated cycle of observing state, deciding, acting, receiving an observation, updating state, and checking whether to stop.
A process whose transitions are substantially predetermined by software even when LLMs perform some steps.
A bounded callable capability through which an agent reads or changes an external system.
The schema, semantics, permissions, failure modes, and side-effect rules of a tool.
The construction of the task-relevant information presented to a model at a particular decision point.
Retrieval-augmented generation: selecting external information and including it in the model context for grounding.
Structured information needed to continue the current task, distinct from the transient model prompt.
Stored information about prior interactions, runs, outcomes, or experiences.
Relatively stable facts, policies, and domain knowledge maintained outside the current task.
A persisted execution state from which a long-running task can safely resume.
The property that repeating an operation does not create duplicate side effects.
Delegation in which another agent becomes responsible for part or all of a task or conversation.
An agent or deterministic controller responsible for routing, delegation, and integrating specialist work.
The ordered sequence of decisions, observations, tool calls, state changes, approvals, and outputs in an agent run.
The empirically supported set of task classes and conditions under which a system meets defined reliability requirements.
A validation or control around inputs, outputs, or tool actions; strong guardrails are backed by enforceable runtime policy.
Instructions embedded in untrusted content that attempt to redirect model behavior or exploit the authority of the surrounding system.
Model Context Protocol, a standard for exposing tools, resources, and related capabilities to AI applications.
Agent2Agent Protocol, a standard for discovery and task-oriented interaction between independent agent systems.
Operational practices for observing, evaluating, controlling, and improving deployed agent systems.
A resumable control point where a consequential proposed action is reviewed before execution.
A model used as an evaluator for semantic criteria; it should be calibrated and not substituted for deterministic checks when those exist.
An internal or external representation used to reason about entities, state, constraints, and possible consequences.
A system that combines learned model reasoning with deterministic rules, solvers, tests, types, or other formal constraints.
